top_categories.workout_context: Road-specific control matters at GFNY Bremen. Practice on flat: use smooth gear and cadence changes, accelerate deliberately out of corners, and settle quickly back into sustainable power for 69 miles.
Race-pace efforts that mimic GFNY Bremen's demands. Pacing, fueling, and tactical decisions under fatigue. Practice the race before August.
When someone attacks on flat, you have 10 seconds to respond or you're off the back. This builds that response.
Brief efforts above sustainable power can come from grade changes, positioning, or closing a gap at GFNY Bremen. Train them without letting those efforts derail the longer pacing plan.
69 miles on flat burns energy faster than the distance suggests. Train the fade resistance now.
GFNY Bremen's flat rewards steady threshold power. Surging and recovering costs more watts than just holding.
2-minute all-out efforts on flat. Closing gaps, responding to attacks, sprinting for position. Train the burn.
88–92% FTP is where you'll spend the hardest sustained miles of GFNY Bremen. Train it until it feels boring.
At GFNY Bremen, changes in grade or pace can lift effort above threshold before it settles again. Over-unders train that transition while you keep riding.
Long rides with hard efforts mixed in. Simulates what GFNY Bremen's flat actually does to you.
Smooth pedaling at 69 miles saves muscle. Bad technique at mile 10 is invisible. At mile 80 it's a cramp.
Double-threshold training builds sustained power with less fatigue. More FTP per hour of training.

race_overlay.nutrition: Use training to rehearse an eating and drinking plan for GFNY Bremen's 69 miles. Start early and use products you tolerate. Use the organizer's current resupply plan for final carry decisions.
race_overlay.terrain: The course profile at GFNY Bremen rewards specific practice. Include regular rides on flat to build confidence.

pack_summary: This 10-workout pack focuses on Road Specific, Race Simulation, and VO2max to prepare you for 69 miles of flat in Bremen, Germany.
